## Introduction

### Background & Relevant Work

There are [18.8 million](https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/food-access-research-atlas/documentation#:~:text=This%20measure%20shows%20that%20an%20estimated%2018.8%20million%20people%2C%20or%206.1%20percent%20of%20the%20U.S.%20population%2C%20live%20in%20low%2Dincome%20and%20low%20access%20tracts%20and%20are%20more%20than%201%20mile%20or%2010%20miles%20from%20a%20supermarket) Americans living in food deserts today — areas with limited access to affordable and nutritious food. The [USDA has defined food deserts](https://www.ers.usda.gov/amber-waves/2011/december/data-feature-mapping-food-deserts-in-the-u-s#:~:text=ERS's%20Food%20Desert%20Locator%20is,are%20defined%20as%20food%20deserts.) to be census tracts that have a poverty rate of 20% or greater (or median family income that is less than 80% of statewide family income) and where at least 33% of the population live more than 1 mile from the supermarket in an urban area/ 10 miles in a rural area. Food deserts are created by distance from healthy food sources, usually influenced by structural decisions that have historically limited healthy food access for minority communities. Understanding this issue requires examining how redlining policies institutionalized neighborhood disinvestment, disproportionately exposing low-income and [minority communities to less healthy food environments](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2024/12/food-deserts-robinson-patman/680765/). These disparities carry serious consequences: food deserts are linked to worse health outcomes, including [shorter life expectancy](https://pressroom.cancer.org/releases?item=1237,) and a higher risk for [adverse cardiovascular events](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6405658/). Given these health risks and the disproportionate racial impact of food deserts, it is critical to evaluate what factors contribute to their persistence and how current policy can work toward reversing years of racial residential segregation.

This issue is particularly relevant to us as Duke students, as [9 of the top 10 states with the greatest share of residents living in food deserts are in the South](https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/food-access-research-atlas/state-level-estimates-of-low-income-and-low-access-populations). In particular, North Carolina is one of the top 10 agricultural states in the US, but its [food insecurity rate is 13.9%](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0330333) — 2.2 percentage points higher than the national average. This proximity makes understanding the structural drivers of food deserts a matter of community concern. Thus, I seek to answer the following question: what features can best explain whether a census tract is a food desert (classified as a low-income, low-access area) in North Carolina?

[Studies](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ypmed.2013.10.010) have found that neighborhood racial composition and poverty rates are associated with food store availability. Interestingly, this study notes that these associations vary by rural and urban regions, which is why interventions should be developed locally rather than universally. A [cross-sectional survey](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pmedr.2019.01.001) of randomly selected households in public housing communities in Baltimore, MD found that indivduals with a personal vehicle were more likely to report ease in reaching health food stores as compared to others.

### Data & Key Variables

I will use the [USDA's 2019 Food Research Atlas](https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/food-access-research-atlas/download-the-data) dataset to investigate my question and choose key predictors to understand patterns of food access in North Carolina. The 2019 Food Access Research Atlas provides an overview of food access indicators in the US by measuring variables like supermarket accessibility, race, poverty rate, and median income. This [dataset is a combination of data](https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/food-access-research-atlas/documentation#data) collected by the 2010 Decennial Census, the 2014-18 American Community Survey (ACS), and two 2019 lists of supermarkets, one being from Trade Dimensions TDLinx. Observations are at the census tract level and therefore may not be independent, as nearby census tracts are likely to exhibit similar patterns in food desert status and food desert predictors. To address this limitation, I will take a random sample of 20% from the North Carolina subset of the dataset.

There is also substantial missing data in the `LALOWI1_10` variable, which represents the amount of people living in a low access, low income area. Thus, I will use the `LILATracts_1AND10` response variable, which is an indicator variable of what `LALOWI1_10` measures — whether a tract is classified as low income and low access (food desert). The `MedianFamilyIncome` variable also has 17 missing observations. However, since this is not a significant portion of the data for the NC sample (17 missing out of 448 observations), I will delete these observations rather than impute counts, so as not to assume patterns for certain areas. As a result, I also acknowledge that this data may not be entirely representative of the entire state, especially if those null values were concentrated in a specific area.

To understand factors that contribute to a census tract's categorization as low-income and low-access (or being a food desert), I will focus on the `LILATracts_1And10` response variable as a proxy measure for food desert (as it fits the [USDA's definition of a food desert](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/IF11841)) and the following predictor variables: `Urban` , `TractSNAP` , `TractHUNV` , `PovertyRate` , `MedianFamilyIncome` . `Urban` is an indicator variable that classifies a census tract as urban or not using the official definition by the US Census (urban area has more than 2,500 people). This predictor will contribute to understanding whether food deserts vary by urbanicity, which is helpful in understanding where policymakers should direct resources to address such issues. Next, `TractSNAP` will detail the number of housing units within a census tract receiving SNAP benefits. The rationale behind including this predictor is that communities with more individuals receiving SNAP benefits are also likely to be underresourced, characteristic of food deserts. `TractHUNV` provides information on number of housing units with access to a vehicle, which could illuminate the low access to grocery stores aspect of the food desert definition. Finally, `MedianFamilyIncome` and `Urban` will both be used to determine the general economic state of families in a census tract.

### Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r}
#| label: clean-data

set.seed(123)

food_access_clean <- food_access |>
  filter(State=="North Carolina" & !is.na(MedianFamilyIncome)) |>
  convert_as_factor(Urban,County, State, LILATracts_1And10) |>
  select(Urban,
         TractSNAP,
         TractHUNV,
         LILATracts_1And10,
         PovertyRate,
         MedianFamilyIncome,
         State,
         County,
         CensusTract) |>
  mutate(CensusTract = as.character(CensusTract),
         Urban = factor(Urban, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Rural", "Urban")),
         LILATracts_1And10 = factor(LILATracts_1And10, levels = c(0, 1),
                                    labels = c("Not Food Desert", "Food Desert"))) |>
  slice_sample(prop = 0.2)


```


The map illustrates how the majorty of North Carolina does not contain areas classified as food deserts. More specifically, it shows that food deserts are concentrated in small areas around the state, and viewed in conjunction with the stacked bar chart, we understand that census tracts classified as food deserts are primarily also categorized as urban areas. To be specific, 84% of census tracts in NC are not food deserts. Due to this class imbalance, it is likely that the model fit on this data will not be accurate at predicting tracts that are food deserts, so I will gear my model selection toward explaining factors that contribute to food deserts.

Each of the quantitative predictors ( `PovertyRate`, `TractSNAP`, `TractHUNV`, `MedianFamilyIncome`) have a unimodal and slightly right-skewed distribution. `Urban` shows a similar pattern of positive skew as the majority of census tracts in North Carolina (around 62%) are classified as urban. To ensure that the relationships between the quantitative predictors and the response is linear, I plotted each against the predicted probability of being a food desert and confirmed linear relationships. This helped me determine not to log-transform the predictors when fitting my logistic regression model.

Due to this skew, the median is a good indicator of the center of the distribution for each of the variables. Thus, we see that the median poverty rate in NC is about 14.30%, which is higher than the [United States' official 10.6% poverty rate](https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2025/demo/p60-287.html). There are also some insignificant outlying census tracts with poverty rates above 50%. On average, 188 housing units in a census tract receive SNAP benefits. The IQR for this distribution is 255 housing units, which seems relatively large, but considering the fact that a census tract can range anywhere from 1,200 to 8,000 people, this spread is understandable. Traditionally, 80 housing units in a census tract do not have access to a vehicle. This is surprisingly low but realistic since a car is a necessity in most parts of NC due to the state's lack of public transportation. The relatively smaller spread (IQR=11) is in line with our understanding of NC's public infrastructure and the necessity of a vehicle, regardless of income status. Finally, `MedianFamilyIncome` has a distribution very similar to `PovertyRate` , which is not unexpected since both are roughly measuring the economic state of a census tract. There is a center around \$61,500 median family income per census tract, much lower than the [US's \$83,000 median household income](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/MEHOINUSA646N). The spread of the distribution (IQR) is about \$20,000, with outliers above median family incomes of \$150,000.

```{r}
#| label: double-density-plot

# income x lila
food_access_clean |>
ggplot(aes(x = MedianFamilyIncome, fill = LILATracts_1And10)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Income Distribution by Food Desert Status",
       x = "Median Family Income by tract",
       fill = "Food Desert Status") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar())
```

The double-density plot reveals that median family income is more variable among food desert tracts than non-food desert tracts. For instance, tracts that are not food deserts have a similar center to tracts that are food deserts, but the median incomes are more spread out from \$45,000 to \$125,000, while median incomes for food desert tracts are mostly concentrated around \$45,000 to \$50,000. This distinction suggests a strong association between median family income and food desert status.

Interestingly, when observing the relationship of the quantitative predictors and the response variable, there are more outliers and a higher spread for non-food desert tracts. This may be due to less uniformity in socioeconomic characteristics among non–food desert tracts.

```{r}

#| message: false
#| fig.keep: "last"

# plot pred probs of food desert and median income by urbanicity
ggplot(food_access_clean, aes(x = MedianFamilyIncome,
                             y = as.numeric(LILATracts_1And10) - 1,
                             color = Urban)) +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2, height = 0.02) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm",
              method.args = list(family = "binomial"),
              se = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Median Family Income × Urban Interaction Effect",
       y = "Probability of Food Desert",
       x = "Median Family Income") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar())

# box plot of median income vs food desert by urbanicity
food_access_clean |>
  ggplot(aes(x = LILATracts_1And10, y = MedianFamilyIncome, fill = Urban)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(title = "Income Distribution by Food Desert Status and Urbanicity",
       y = "Median Family Income",
       x = "Food Desert Classification") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar())

# interaction between SNAP and poverty rate

food_access_clean |>
  mutate(bin_SNAP = factor(ntile(TractSNAP, 3),
                           labels = c("Low SNAP", "Mid SNAP", "High SNAP"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = PovertyRate, 
             y = as.numeric(LILATracts_1And10) - 1,
             color = bin_SNAP)) +
    geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2, height = 0.02) +
    geom_smooth(method = "glm",
                method.args = list(family = "binomial"),
                se = FALSE) +
    labs(title = "SNAP × Poverty Rate Interaction Effect",
         y = "Probability of Food Desert",
         x = "Poverty Rate",
         color = "SNAP Recipients") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1))

```

My key variables assess the geographic makeup of a tract (`Urban)` as well as poverty or economic status of individuals within the tract (`MedianFamilyIncome` , `PovertyRate` , `TractHUNV` , and `TractSNAP` ). Since SNAP benefits are determined by relative income level and poverty rate, I visualize the interaction between the number of households receiving snap benefits in a tract and the tract poverty rate. According to the plot, there appears to be an interaction effect, as the slopes of the lines — representing different levels of snap receipt — differ. Most interesting is that tracts with a high number of SNAP recipients do not see as drastic an increase in the probability of being a food desert as poverty rate increases, as compared to tracts with a low number of SNAP recipients. This pattern could be explained by the fact that if a tract has a high number of households receiving SNAP benefits, then it is already more likely to be classified as a food desert, hence the flatter slope as poverty rate increases. For tracts with a low number of households receiving SNAP benefits, poverty rate then serves as an important metric of food desert status, which could explain the sharp increase in probability of being a food desert with each 1 percentage point increase in poverty rate.

In working with health and social science data, I am also cognizant of confounding being a limitation. This dataset does not provide a comprehensive account of all the factors that impact whether a census tract is a food desert since other variables can influence this measure/ the measure of other predictors. For instance, the `TractHUNV` predictor measures the number of housing units without a vehicle in a certain tract. Though the absence of a vehicle can make healthy food inaccessible, and therefore contribute to the categorization of an area as a food desert, the variable does not give a complete picture of accessibility — especially since access to public transportation is not considered. I will remain mindful of these limitations and incorporate them into my interpretation of the model to ensure that my conclusions are statistically sound and representative of the data.

## Methodology

```{r}
#| label: transformations
#| fig.show: "hide"

# - check if log transformation necessary by comparing pred binning vs logins (odds of being a food desert). If it levels off then log transform.

# check for linear relationship between TractHUNV and food desert
 p1 <- food_access_clean |>
  mutate(
    y = as.numeric(LILATracts_1And10) - 1,
    # ntile code from: https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/ntile.html
    hunv_bin = ntile(TractHUNV, 10) 
  ) |>
  group_by(hunv_bin) |>
  # code in the summarize and following mutate function adapted from ChatGPT
  summarise(
    hunv_mid = mean(TractHUNV, na.rm = TRUE),
    p = mean(y, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # smooth to avoid p = 0 or 1
    p_adj = (p * (n - 1) + 0.5) / n,
    log_odds = log(p_adj / (1 - p_adj))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hunv_mid, y = log_odds)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Housing Units without Vehicle",
    y = "Log-Odds of Food Desert",
    title = "Linearity Check: HUNV vs Log-Odds"
  )
 
 
p2 <- food_access_clean |>
  mutate(
    y = as.numeric(LILATracts_1And10) - 1,
    # ntile code from: https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/ntile.html
    hunv_bin = ntile(log1p(TractHUNV), 10) 
  ) |>
  group_by(hunv_bin) |>
  # code in the summarize and following mutate function adapted from ChatGPT
  summarise(
    hunv_mid = mean(log1p(TractHUNV), na.rm = TRUE),
    p = mean(y, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # smooth to avoid p = 0 or 1
    p_adj = (p * (n - 1) + 0.5) / n,
    log_odds = log(p_adj / (1 - p_adj))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = hunv_mid, y = log_odds)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = " LOGGED: Housing Units without Vehicle",
    y = "Log-Odds of Food Desert",
    title = "Linearity Check: HUNV vs Log-Odds"
  ) 
p1 | p2
 
 

# check for linear relationship between PovertyRate and food desert
food_access_clean |>
  mutate(
    y = as.numeric(LILATracts_1And10) - 1,
    # ntile code from: https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/ntile.html
    povertyRate_bin = ntile(PovertyRate, 10)
  ) |>
  group_by(povertyRate_bin) |>
  # code in the summarize and following mutate function adapted from ChatGPT
  summarise(
    povertyRate_mid = mean(PovertyRate, na.rm = TRUE),
    p = mean(y, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # smooth to avoid p = 0 or 1
    p_adj = (p * (n - 1) + 0.5) / n,
    log_odds = log(p_adj / (1 - p_adj))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = povertyRate_mid, y = log_odds)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Poverty Rate",
    y = "Log-Odds of Food Desert",
    title = "Linearity Check: Poverty Rate vs Log-Odds"
  )

# check for linear relationship between TractSNAP and food desert
food_access_clean |>
  mutate(
    y = as.numeric(LILATracts_1And10) - 1,
    # ntile code from: https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/ntile.html
    SNAP_bin = ntile(TractSNAP, 10)
  ) |>
  group_by(SNAP_bin) |>
   # code in the summarize and following mutate function adapted from ChatGPT
  summarise(
    SNAP_mid = mean(TractSNAP, na.rm = TRUE),
    p = mean(y, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # smooth to avoid p = 0 or 1
    p_adj = (p * (n - 1) + 0.5) / n,
    log_odds = log(p_adj / (1 - p_adj))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = SNAP_mid, y = log_odds)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Tract SNAP",
    y = "Log-Odds of Food Desert",
    title = "Linearity Check: Tract SNAP vs Log-Odds"
  )

# check for linear relationship between income and food desert
food_access_clean |>
  mutate(
    y = as.numeric(LILATracts_1And10) - 1,
    # ntile code from: https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/ntile.html
    income_bin = ntile(MedianFamilyIncome, 10)
  ) |>
  group_by(income_bin) |>
  # code in the summarize and following mutate function adapted from ChatGPT
  summarise(
    income_mid = mean(MedianFamilyIncome, na.rm = TRUE),
    p = mean(y, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # smooth to avoid p = 0 or 1
    p_adj = (p * (n - 1) + 0.5) / n,
    log_odds = log(p_adj / (1 - p_adj))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = income_mid, y = log_odds)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Median Family Income",
    y = "Log-Odds of Food Desert",
    title = "Linearity Check: Median Family Income vs Log-Odds"
  )

```

```{r}
#| label: fit-model
#| output: false

baseline_fit <-  glm(LILATracts_1And10 ~ 
                       Urban,
                     data = food_access_clean,
                     family = "binomial")

model_poverty <- glm(LILATracts_1And10 ~ 
                     MedianFamilyIncome +
                     TractSNAP +
                     TractHUNV +
                     PovertyRate,
                   data = food_access_clean,
                   family = "binomial")

model_combined <-  glm(LILATracts_1And10 ~ 
                     MedianFamilyIncome +
                     Urban +
                     TractSNAP +
                     TractHUNV +
                     PovertyRate,
                   data = food_access_clean,
                   family = "binomial")

model_urban_income_interact <- glm(LILATracts_1And10 ~ 
                     MedianFamilyIncome * Urban +
                     TractSNAP +
                     TractHUNV +
                     PovertyRate,
                   data = food_access_clean,
                   family = "binomial")

model_snap_poverty_interact <-  glm(LILATracts_1And10 ~ 
                     MedianFamilyIncome +
                     Urban +
                     TractSNAP * PovertyRate +
                     TractHUNV,
                   data = food_access_clean,
                   family = "binomial")

model_urban_hunv_interact <-  glm(LILATracts_1And10 ~ 
                     MedianFamilyIncome +
                     TractSNAP +
                     TractHUNV * PovertyRate +
                     Urban,
                   data = food_access_clean,
                   family = "binomial")

AIC(baseline_fit)
AIC(model_poverty)
AIC(model_combined) # very close to smallest AIC
AIC(model_urban_income_interact)
AIC(model_snap_poverty_interact) # smallest AIC
AIC(model_urban_hunv_interact)


BIC(baseline_fit)
BIC(model_poverty)

BIC(model_snap_poverty_interact) # second smallest BIC
BIC(model_urban_hunv_interact)
```

We will fit a logistic regression model to predict what factors contribute to food deserts across counties in North Carolina. This model is best suited for my dataset because I wish to predict whether a specific census tract is or is not classified as a food desert. Since this is represented as a probability of being a food desert (binary choice), logistic regression will help make such a prediction. To select an explanatory model, I calculated AIC and BIC for the following models. $$ \text{1. Geographical Model: } \log\left(\frac{\hat{\pi}_i}{1-\hat{\pi}_i}\right) = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \cdot \text{Urban}_i $$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{2. Poverty Model: }\log\left(\frac{\hat{\pi}_i}{1 - \hat{\pi}_i}\right) = &\; \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \cdot \text{MedianIncome}_i + \hat{\beta}_2 \cdot \text{SNAP}_i \\&+ \hat{\beta}_3 \cdot \text{HUNV}_i + \hat{\beta}_4 \cdot \text{PovertyRate}_i\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{3. Combined Model: }\log\left(\frac{\hat{\pi}_i}{1 - \hat{\pi}_i}\right) = &\; \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \cdot \text{Urban}_i + \hat{\beta}_2 \cdot \text{MedianIncome}_i \\
&+ \hat{\beta}_3 \cdot \text{SNAP}_i + \hat{\beta}_4 \cdot \text{HUNV}_i + \hat{\beta}_5 \cdot \text{PovertyRate}_i
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{4. Interaction Model: } \log\left(\frac{\hat{\pi}_i}{1-\hat{\pi}_i}\right) = &\; \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 \cdot \text{Urban}_i + \hat{\beta}_2 \cdot \text{MedianIncome}_i \\
&+ \hat{\beta}_3 \cdot \text{SNAP}_i + \hat{\beta}_4 \cdot \text{HUNV}_i + \hat{\beta}_5 \cdot \text{PovertyRate}_i \\
&+ \hat{\beta}_6(\text{SNAP}_i \times \text{PovertyRate}_i)
\end{aligned}$$

$$
\text{where } \hat{\pi}_i \text{ represents the probability a census tract is a food desert}
$$

Testing each of these models allowed me to understand which interactions and predictors were most helpful in explaining the existence of a food desert census tract in NC. AIC/BIC revealed that the models with the lowest scores were the combined model (AIC: 255.682; BIC: 280.0789 ) and the interaction model (AIC: 255.481; BIC: 283.944). Since the difference in AIC was negligible — and BIC prioritizes prediction and parsimonious models — I used variance inflation factors and a drop in deviance test to further confirm which model to use. Computing the variance inflation factors for both models revealed no multicollinearity. Finally, to understand if the interaction effect is truly a necessary addition for explaining variation in predicted probabilities of a food desert tract, I conducted a drop-in-deviance test. The test showed a p-value of 0.138, which is greater than the significance threshold of 0.05 and therefore not a significant impact. Hence, I selected the final model to be the combined model with as `Urban` , `MedianFamilyIncome` , `TractSNAP`, `TractHUNV`, and `PovertyRate` as predictors.

&+ \hat{\beta}_3 \cdot \text{SNAP}_i + \hat{\beta}_4 \cdot \text{HUNV}_i + \hat{\beta}_5 \cdot \text{PovertyRate}_i

### Model assumptions and diagnostics

Logistic regression requires that observations are independent, that the log-odds of the outcome have a linear relationship with continuous predictors, and that there is no severe multicollinearity among predictors. The independence assumption is partially addressed by our random 20% sample of North Carolina census tracts, which reduces (though does not eliminate) the spatial dependence among neighboring tracts. I binned and plotted each quantitative predictor against the log odds of being a food desert and found a straight, linear relationship for each. This pattern confirmed the fulfillment of the model conditions for linearity in log odds. Regarding multicollinearity, the VIF scores for the final model were all below about 3.5, indicating no problematic collinearity among the predictors. Finally, Cook's distance confirmed no influential outliers that would affect model fit.

### Model Fit

```{r}
#| label: model-fit

# chi square test of overall model fit
# from https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/152358/clarification-on-null-hypothesis-w-r-t
#-pchisq-function-in-r-and-the-tail-arg
pchisq(model_combined$null.deviance - model_combined$deviance,
       model_combined$df.null - model_combined$df.residual,
       lower.tail = FALSE)

# AUC
roc_curve <- roc(food_access_clean$LILATracts_1And10, fitted(model_combined))
auc(roc_curve)
plot(roc_curve, 
     print.auc = TRUE,          
     col = "blue",
     main = "ROC Curve - Combined Model")
```

A chi-squared test was done to assess how useful the model is compared to the null — model with no predictors. The result of 8.472432e-27 \< 0.05, so it is significant and we can conclude that the final model fits significantly better than the null (intercept-only) model. The ROC curve above also demonstrates how well the final model distinguishes between the binary outcomes of being a food desert vs. not being a food desert. At an AUC of 0.890, we can conclude that the model distinguishes well between classes.

### Interpretation

`MedianFamilyIncome` is a statistically significant predictor, indicating that for every \$1,000 increase in median family income, the odds of being a food desert decrease by about 7.7%, holding all else constant. This pattern is in line with previous studies and expectations for income to play a role in determining odds of food deserts.

`TractSNAP` is also statistically significant, showing for each additional household receiving SNAP benefits in a tract, the odds that the tract is a food desert are expected to increase by 0.3% on average, holding all else constant. This positive association suggests that higher SNAP participation is linked to greater food access limitations, showing that financial assistance alone may not fully address barriers to accessing healthy food. However, the impact of `TractSNAP` variable is not as large as we would have expected, suggesting that it might not have as large of an impact on determining food desert status.

`Urban` is another statistically signficant predictor. It demonstrates that the odds of an urban tract being classified as a food desert are 14.67 times the odds of a rural tract. This phenomenon is exactly what we noticed in the EDA where many food desert tracts were urban.

Altogether, the model suggests that economic measures, such as median family income and SNAP benefit receipt, are the most consistent predictors of food desert classification among North Carolina census tracts. The role of the other predictors is more complex, since the higher p-values do not allow us to comment on the significance of those predictors and patterns they illuminate about food access.

## Discussion

This analysis found that both economic and geographic factors like median family income, SNAP benefit receipt, and urbanicity are the strongest predictors of food desert classification among North Carolina census tracts. These results align with prior research that suggests neighborhood location and poverty rates are closely tied to food access limitations. It is especially important to note the finding that urban tracts in NC have 14.67 times the odds of being classified as food deserts compared to rural tracts because it challenges my hypothesis and the commonly held assumption that food deserts primarily occur in rural areas. This phenomenon points to urban disinvestment shaping food access. Furthermore, the relationship between SNAP participation and food desert status shows how government programs aimed at improving food access are insufficient to overcome structural barriers to food access.

This study contains several limitations. Most notably, the 20% random sample reduces spatial correlation between tracts, but it is not a method to fully eliminate dependence among neighboring census tracts, which could affect the reliability of model predictions. Additionally, the class imbalance with only 16% of tracts classified as food deserts may limit the model's ability to detect important predictors of food desert status. Future work could address these limitations by using statistical methods to account for geographic clustering. Additionally, including variables relating to demographics like race, ethnicity, and age could illuminate the relevance of different categories of predictors — beyond economic or geographical.
